scenes.visual: Static wide shot on a cream background. A single white card with rounded corners sits on the left. A gold and black circular logo is in the bottom left corner.

scenes.label: Opening Hook
scenes.visual: A second dark gray card appears in the center. A teal arrow connects the left card to this new center card.

scenes.audio: Does buying life insurance remove the risk of death? No. It transfers specified financial consequences under a contract. To classify a risk management action, ask what changes. Does the person avoid an exposure, keep the financial responsibility, share it, reduce the chance or size of loss, or transfer specified costs? One family can use several methods together. The name of the action matters less than what that action actually accomplishes.
scenes.label: Product Information
scenes.visual: A third white card appears on the right. A teal arrow connects the center card to the right card. The layout remains static for the duration.

scenes.audio: Consider three decisions. Marcus chooses not to take part in recreational rock climbing. He avoids that particular exposure, although he has not avoided every risk in life. He installs a handrail on a slippery stairway. That reduces the likelihood of a fall; it does not guarantee safety. He also decides to pay for small, affordable losses from his own savings. That is retention. Retention may be intentional or result from simply having no insurance. Savings finance a loss; they do not prevent it.
scenes.label: Usage Scenarios
scenes.visual: Graphic shifts to three cards side-by-side. The center card features a teal top border. Background remains cream with a teal top bar.

scenes.audio: Sharing spreads a financial burden among participants. Pooling illustrates that idea across a group. Transfer moves a specified financial obligation to another party, often through insurance.
scenes.label: Usage Scenarios
scenes.visual: Two cards are displayed side-by-side. The left card is white, and the right card is light gray/teal.

scenes.audio: Marcus buys a policy that pays a stated benefit for a covered death. His family still experiences the loss of a person, while the insurer has the contractual payment obligation. Insurance does not transfer every possible consequence, and exclusions or limits still matter. Sharing and transfer can both appear in the same insurance arrangement at different levels. Insurance works best with many similar exposure units and losses that are accidental from the insured's perspective, definite enough to identify and measure in financial terms. The probability and cost must be reasonably estimable and the premium economically feasible. Large, correlated catastrophes can strain a pool, so insurers manage concentration. These are useful characteristics, not a promise that every risk meeting a checklist will be accepted. Pure risk offers loss or no loss. Speculative risk also offers possible gain, such as buying stock hoping its price rises.
scenes.label: Usage Scenarios
scenes.visual: Three cards side-by-side. The middle card has a distinct thin gold border on its top edge.

scenes.audio: Now follow a different contract. An insurer accepts Marcus's policy, then arranges for a reinsurer to take part of its insurance risk. This is reinsurance. The original insurer is the ceding insurer. The other company is the reinsurer. Unless a separate legal arrangement changes the policy obligation, Marcus's insurer still owes the policy benefit. He does not normally file part of his claim with the reinsurer. Reinsurance can help manage large individual exposures, accumulated losses, and the insurer's capacity to write business.
scenes.label: Usage Scenarios
scenes.visual: Flowchart graphic with three cards connected by teal arrows. The central card is dark gray, flanked by two white cards.

scenes.audio: Imagine a family maintains safe stairs, holds an emergency fund, and purchases life insurance. The stairs reduce a hazard. The fund supports retained costs. The policy transfers covered financial risk. If the insurer buys reinsurance, that creates another transfer between insurers. On a question, locate the parties and the event first. Then identify the action's effect. Do not call every sensible precaution avoidance, and do not assume every transfer erases the underlying danger. Answer the lesson questions using those distinctions.
